title: Demo: Should we always tell the truth?

elements.text: Should we always tell the truth?
Yes: truthfulness is an unconditional duty
A lie cannot become a universal law: it would destroy all trust in what people say
The moral worth of an act lies in its principle, not in its consequences
The murderer at the door: even to him, I must not lie
Telling the truth is a duty only towards those who have a right to the truth
“Right to the truth” ≠ right to truthfulness: the first expression is meaningless
elements.source: Kant, On a Supposed Right to Lie

elements.text: Whoever lies answers for the consequences of the lie; whoever tells the truth does not

steps.title: The question
steps.narration: Lying to save a friend: is it still wrong? In 1797, Benjamin Constant and Kant disagree on this very case.

steps.title: Kant’s answer
steps.narration: **Yes, always.** For Kant, truthfulness is an unconditional duty: no circumstance makes lying permissible.

steps.title: Why?
steps.narration: A maxim that allowed lying could not become a **universal law**: if everyone lied whenever it suited them, no one would believe anyone, and a given word would mean nothing. A **reductio**: universalised, lying destroys itself.

steps.title: What it presupposes
steps.narration: The thesis rests on an **assumption**: the moral worth of an act lies in its **principle**, not in its consequences. The cloud marks a belief that is often implicit, yet debatable; here, a normative one.

steps.title: The murderer at the door
steps.narration:
> A murderer asks me whether my friend, whom he is pursuing, has taken refuge in my house.

Even to him, Kant says, I must not lie.

steps.title: Constant’s objection
steps.narration:
> To tell the truth is therefore a duty only towards those who have a right to the truth. But no one has a right to a truth that harms others.

Benjamin Constant, *On Political Reactions* (1797).

steps.title: A distinction
steps.narration: Kant first answers with a **distinction**: to speak of a “right to the truth” is meaningless; one only has a right to **truthfulness**, to not being lied to. The objection rests on a confusion. *On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy* (1797).

steps.title: The consequences
steps.narration: Kant holds his ground: if I lie, I become responsible for everything that follows; if I tell the truth, what happens cannot be imputed to me.

steps.title: Overview
steps.narration: Two moralities meet: one of **duty**, one of **consequences**. The shape of each box tells its type, its color its function; press L to show the legend.
